claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain and toughness in polycrystalline tungsten-based alloys are governed by grain-boundary character.
A higher fraction of high-angle grain boundaries promotes dislocation climb.
A higher fraction of high-angle grain boundaries promotes grain-boundary sliding.
High-angle grain boundaries increase high-temperature plastic strain.
High-angle grain boundaries reduce toughness by weakening resistance to crack propagation.
Predominantly low-angle grain boundaries impede dislocation motion.
Predominantly low-angle grain boundaries enhance toughness.
The toughness enhancement associated with low-angle boundaries occurs at the expense of plastic deformation.

Thermo-mechanical grain-boundary engineering can create tungsten-based alloy microstructures enriched in either high-angle or low-angle grain boundaries while grain size and other features are controlled.
Between 1200°C and 1500°C, dislocation climb is operative in the proposed tungsten-based alloys.
High-angle-boundary-enriched samples will exhibit greater plastic strain than the conventionally processed baseline.
High-angle-boundary-enriched samples will exhibit lower toughness than the conventionally processed baseline.
Low-angle-boundary-enriched samples will exhibit lower plastic strain and greater toughness.
The proposed relationship should hold below the melting point when dislocation climb is dominant and grain size and secondary microstructural factors are controlled.
Subgrain formation and minor secondary phases may independently influence high-temperature deformation and toughness.
